title: Chirurgie des surfaces conformes : notes manuscrites (s.d., 1983-1984), lettres (1984).

deep.reconstruction:
This is section 12) of Grothendieck's notes on 'chirurgie des surfaces conformes', titled 'Récapitulation'. It summarises the preceding pages on canonical metrics.

Setting. X is a conformal surface without boundary. As the neighbouring pages show (inversions, Aut^+, the real projective plane), this includes non-orientable surfaces, i.e. dianalytic or Klein-type structures.

Claim. On X one can define a canonical Riemannian metric Q_X compatible with the conformal structure, except in two cases.

Case (a): X ≅ C, i.e. X is an affine line over a topological field abstractly isomorphic to C. Here one can only define a class of compatible metrics up to a positive scalar. These are the translation-invariant metrics, which are exactly the metrics carried to scalar multiples of themselves by every conformal automorphism z ↦ az+b (and conjugates). They are flat.

Case (b): X ≅ P^1_C, i.e. a projective line over such a field, or a conformal sphere.
- There is no Riemannian metric invariant under G = Aut(X), nor even under Aut^+(X) ≅ PSL_2(C), which is non-compact.
- There is, however, the set R(X) of 'normalised spherical' metrics: round metrics compatible with the conformal structure and of total area 1. R(X) is a single G-orbit.
- The margin note says R(X) is a homogeneous manifold of dimension 3. In modern terms R(X) = PSL_2(C)/SO(3) = hyperbolic 3-space H^3, whose ideal boundary is X.
- For a subgroup H ⊂ G: there is an H-invariant Q ∈ R(X) iff H is relatively compact. In modern terms this is the Cartan fixed-point theorem for H acting isometrically on H^3, plus the fact that a group with a bounded orbit is relatively compact.
- Such a Q is unique iff X^H = ∅. Reason: the fixed set of a compact H in H^3 is a totally geodesic subspace. If it has positive dimension it contains a geodesic, whose ideal endpoints are fixed by H. Conversely, if H fixes a point x in H^3 and a boundary point p, it fixes the ray from x to p pointwise, so the fixed set is not a single point.
- When X^H ≠ ∅, the preceding page determines R(X)^H. Either #X^H = 2, and R(X)^H is a geodesic, parametrised by T-orbits in X∖X^H. Or H = {1, σ} with σ an inversion, and R(X)^H is a totally geodesic plane, parametrised by (X∖X^σ)/σ.

Purpose. To fix, for every conformal surface (and every compact symmetry group H in the sphere case), a canonical metric Q_X or Q_{X,H}. The next page lists the resulting cases:
- hyperbolic surfaces get curvature −1;
- surfaces with universal cover ≅ C get flat metrics;
- the real projective plane gets a round metric;
- the sphere with a finite H having no fixed point also gets a round metric.
The aim is presumably to cut and glue conformal surfaces ('chirurgie') with metrically controlled pieces.
errors: As transcribed, case a) says the flat metrics on C are 'inv. par tt automorphisme conforme'. Strictly, the dilations z ↦ az+b with |a| ≠ 1 only multiply such a metric by |a|^2; only the homothety class is invariant. The unclear word in the manuscript may well be 'quasi-inv.', which would make the statement correct.

'Q unique ssi X^H = ∅' is stated only after assuming H relatively compact, which the sentence requires implicitly. With that reading the statement is correct, including for orientation-reversing H such as the antipodal involution, which fixes exactly one point of H^3.

'Canonique' for tori, cylinders and similar cases needs a normalisation: area 1 for tori, a length normalisation for C^*. This is addressed only on the next page, where Q_X is said to be 'défini à cte' in the flat cases.
The previous page marks the detailed classification 'à vérifier'. The recap's claims are nevertheless correct.

ideas.what: Canonical conformally compatible metric on every conformal (possibly non-orientable) surface, with exactly two exceptions: C, where it is defined only up to scale, and P^1, where it does not exist.
ideas.modern_name: Uniformization; canonical constant-curvature metric (Poincaré metric for hyperbolic surfaces)
ideas.where_published: Possibly alluded to around the 'Esquisse d'un programme' discussion of conformal and Teichmüller towers; not explicitly

ideas.what: Normalised round metrics of area 1 on the conformal sphere form one orbit under Aut, a homogeneous 3-manifold.
ideas.modern_name: Identification of conformal round metrics on S^2 with hyperbolic 3-space H^3 = PSL_2(C)/SO(3)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Poincaré, Klein); used systematically by Thurston and in Douady–Earle (1986)

ideas.what: A subgroup H fixes a round metric iff it is relatively compact; the fixed metric is unique iff H has no fixed point on the sphere.
ideas.modern_name: Cartan fixed-point theorem on H^3; fixed sets of compact isometry groups are totally geodesic

ideas.what: Field-free description: C as an affine line, and P^1 as a projective line, over a topological field abstractly isomorphic to C (no chosen isomorphism, hence no chosen orientation).
ideas.modern_name: Torsor and canonical-structure viewpoint on conformal planes and spheres

missed.claim: Grothendieck picks a canonical round metric on a conformal sphere through an equivariance and fixed-point argument on the 3-dimensional homogeneous space R(X) ≅ H^3. This is the same mechanism (a canonical point of H^3 attached to symmetric data on S^2) later used in the Douady–Earle conformal barycenter (1986). Here it is used to give conformal surfaces with symmetries canonical metrics for surgery. It is a mild anticipation of a standard idea, not a new result.
missed.quote: Il y a pourtant sur X un ens. R(X) de métriques riemanniennes (dites "sphériques normalisées") ... qui forment une orbite sous G ... NB R(X) est variété homogène de dim 3
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mostly of historical interest: it shows Grothendieck using hyperbolic 3-space implicitly as the parameter space of round metrics in his conformal surgery project. The mathematics itself is classical.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a correct and clean summary of classical uniformization and of round metrics on the sphere as points of H^3, with a fixed-point and uniqueness criterion for compact symmetry groups. It is elegantly phrased in Grothendieck's equivariant style, but contains nothing a specialist would find new.
transcription_corrections: '(i.e. X droite affine sur un corps top/C isom. à C)' is more likely 'corps top. isom. à C', meaning a topological field isomorphic to C.
'qui sont aussi celles [?] inv. par tt automorphisme' possibly reads 'qui sont aussi quasi-inv. par tt automorphisme', i.e. invariant up to a scalar.
Margin: 'NB R(X) est [une] variété homogène de dim 3'; the extra word is hard to read.
